The load factor for the structure of a normal category airplane must be able to sustain 3.8 times its weight. This means that for every pound of weight added to a normal category aircraft, the structure must be strong enough to support 3.8 pounds.

In comparison, the load factor for a utility category airplane is 4.4 times its weight, and for an acrobatic category airplane, it is 6.0 times its weight. Therefore, the structure of a normal category airplane is designed to handle less severe conditions than utility or acrobatic category airplanes.

The load factor is a critical design consideration for aircraft, as excessive weight can reduce efficiency and available safety margin. The structure of an airplane must be strong enough to support the maximum allowable weight, as well as the dynamic loads imposed by flight maneuvers.

Weight Control 
Weight is a major factor in airplane construction and 
operation, and it demands respect from all pilots and 
particular diligence by all maintenance personnel. Excessive 
weight reduces the efficiencyof an aircraft and the available 
safety margin if an emergency condition should arise.
When an aircraft is designed, it is made as light as the 
required structural strength allows, and the wings or rotors are 
designed to support the maximum allowable weight. When 
the weight of an aircraft is increased, the wings or rotors must 
produce additional lift and the structure must support not 
only the additional static loads, but also the dynamic loads 
imposed by flight maneuvers. For example, the wings of a 
3,000-pound airplane must support 3,000 pounds in level 
flight, but when the airplane is turned smoothly and sharply 
using a bank angle of 60°, the dynamic load requires the 
wings to support twice this or 6,000 pounds.
Severe uncoordinated maneuvers or flight into turbulence 
can impose dynamic loads on the structure great enough 
to cause failure. In accordance with Title 14 of the Code

Weight Control for Aircraft Other Than 
Fixed and Rotor-wing
Some light aircraft utilize different methods of determining 
weight and balance from the traditional fixedand rotor-wing 
aircraft. These aircraft achieve flight control by methods 
different from the fixed-wing airplane or helicopter. Most 
notable of these are weight-shift control (WSC) aircraft (also 
known as trikes), powered parachutes, and balloons. These 
aircraft typically do not specify either an EWCG or a CG 
range. They require only a certified or approved maximum 
weight. To understand why this is so, a look at how flight
control is achieved is helpful.
Airplanes and WSC aircraft control flightunder the influenc  
of the same four forces (lift, gravity, thrust, and drag), and 
around the same three axes (pitch, yaw, and roll). However, 
each aircraft accomplishes this control in a very different 
manner. This difference helps explain why the fixed-wing
airplane requires an established weight and a known CG, 
whereas the WSC aircraft only requires the known weight.
The fixed-wing airplane has movable controls that alter lift 
on various airfoil surfaces to vary pitch, roll, and yaw. In 
turn, these changes in lift affect the characteristics of the 
flight parameters. Weight normally decreases in flight due 
to fuel consumption, and the airplane CG changes with this

Weight and Balance
Aircraft such as balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC do 
not require weight and balance computations because the load 
is suspended below the lifting mechanism. The CG range in 
these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG 
limits. For example, the rear seat position and fuel of a WSC 
aircraft are as close as possible to the hang point with the 
aircraft in a suspended attitude. Thus, load variations have 
little effect on the CG. This also holds true for lighter-than-
air aircraft, such as a balloon basket or gondola. While it is 
difficult to exceed CG limits in these aircraft, pilots should 
never overload an aircraft, as doing so may cause structural 
damage and/or failures. 
Weight affects performance; therefore, pilots should calculate 
weight and remain within the manufacturer’s established 
limits at all times.
WSC Aircraft
WSC aircraft are one- and two-place aircraft that exceed the 
criteria of an ultra-light vehicle but do meet the criteria of an 
LSA. The definitionfor WSC can be found in 14 CFR part 1.

Airplanes with tandem seating normally have a limitation 
requiring solo flight to be made from the front seat in some

As an aircraft ages, its weight usually increases due to debris 
and dirt collecting in hard-to-reach locations and moisture 
absorbed in the cabin insulation. This increase in weight is 
normally small, but it can be determined only by accurately 
weighing the aircraft.
Changes of fixed equipment may have a major effect upon 
the weight of the aircraft. Many aircraft are overloaded by 
the installation of extra radios or instruments. Fortunately,

This period may be reduced by an airworthiness authority dependent on the conditions of use. However, if no manufacturer’s schedule is available, the period between calibrations should not exceed 12 months.

Scale Preparation

weigh aircraft and are typically cheaper than the platform 
type.Using load cell scales allows for the aircraft to be set

the aircraft is placed on jacks with electronic load cells 
placed between the jack and the jack pad on the aircraft. 
The aircraft is raised on the jacks until the wheels or skids

Determining the Empty Weight and 
Empty Weight CG (EWCG)
When the aircraft is properly prepared for weighing, roll it 
onto the scales, and level it. The weights are measured at 
three weighing points: the two main wheel points and the 
nosewheel point. The empty weight and empty weight CG 
(EWCG) are determined by using the following steps with 
the results recorded in the weight and balance record for use 
in all future weight and balance computations.
1.	
Determine the moment index of each of the main-
wheel points by multiplying the net weight (scale 
reading minus tare weight), in pounds, at these points 
by the distance from the datum, in inches. Divide these 
numbers by the appropriate reduction factor.
2.	
Determine the moment index of the nosewheel 
weighing point by multiplying its net weight, in 
pounds, by its distance from the datum, in inches. 
Divide this by the reduction factor.
3.	
Determine the total weight by adding the net weight of 
the three weighing points and the total moment index 
by adding the moment indexes of each point.
4.	
Divide the total moment index by the total weight and 
multiply the result by the reduction factor. This gives 
the CG in inches from the datum.
5.	
Determine the distance of the CG behind the leading 
edge of the mean aerodynamic chord (LEMAC) 
by subtracting the distance between the datum and 
LEMAC from the distance between the

undergone extensive repair or major alteration, when the pilot

The airframe and powerplant (A&P) FAA-certificated

2.

(EWCG) data in the current approved aircraft flight
manual or issued operating limitations.

The manual does not provide a direct answer to the specific question of how much a U.S. gallon of Jet A weighs at 59 °F according to the standard weights table. However, it does provide some relevant information that can help us determine the answer.

According to the manual, the nominal specific gravity of Jet A fuel is 0.812 at +15 °C (59 °F). However, the weight of Jet A fuel at 59 °F is not explicitly stated in the manual.

The manual does provide the density variation of aviation fuel chart (Figure 9-44), which shows that at 25 °C (77 °F), Jet A fuel weighs 6.75 lb/gal. However, this chart does not provide information for 59 °F.

The manual also provides a table of standard fuels and weights with temperatures of 32 °F and 59 °F (Figure 3-4), but this table only lists the weights of AVGAS (Aviation Gasoline) and JET A & A-1 at 59 °F, which are 6.68 lb/gal and 6.75 lb/gal, respectively.

Based on the information provided in the manual, it is not possible to determine the exact weight of a U.S. gallon of Jet A fuel at 59 °F. However, the closest estimate would be 6.68 lb/gal, but this value is not explicitly stated as the weight of Jet A fuel at 59 °F.

It is also important to note that the manual recommends using the fuel at least 2 hours after it has come up to temperature, and to avoid using scales in temperature extremes below 40 °F or above 100 °F unless the scale is specifically designed for use in those temperatures.

To determine the minimum fuel required for a forward adverse-load CG check, the following steps are outlined:

1. The minimum fuel is calculated as the quantity needed for one-half hour of operation at rated maximum continuous power.
2. This is considered to be 1/12 gallon for each maximum except takeoff (METO) horsepower.
3. Since aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon, the minimum fuel weight is determined by dividing the METO horsepower by 2.

For example, if the METO horsepower is 230, the minimum fuel weight would be:

Minimum fuel weight = (230 METO HP / 2) x 6 pounds/gallon
= 69 pounds

However, the manual provides a specific example where the minimum fuel weight is 115 pounds, which is likely a specific case or a default value.

To find the minimum fuel weight for a specific aircraft, the METO horsepower should be used to calculate the minimum fuel weight as described above.

Note: The manual does not explicitly state that the minimum fuel weight is 115 pounds for all cases, but it provides this value as an example or a specific case.

When a large aircraft's operational empty weight (OEW) must be reestablished by calculation between reweighings, this occurs under the following circumstances:

* **Cumulative change in weight and balance log:**  When the cumulative change to the weight and balance log exceeds plus or minus one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the maximum landing weight.
* **Cumulative change in CG position:** When the cumulative change in the center of gravity (CG) position exceeds one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the MAC (Maximum Allowable CG). For aircraft without a MAC-based CG envelope (e.g., canard equipped airplanes), this limit is applied to the total CG range.

Additionally, OEW should be reestablished by calculation whenever:

* The aircraft undergoes extensive repair or major alteration.
* The pilot reports unsatisfactory flight characteristics (e.g., nose or tail heaviness).
* There are suspicions that recorded weight and balance data are in error.

**Important Notes:**

* Weight changes computed between reweighing periods require knowledge of the weight and CG location of the modifications.
* If this information is not available, the aircraft must be reweighed.
* It is crucial to maintain accurate weight and balance records, but these records are reliable for only limited periods.
* Regular aircraft weighing is essential to ensure safety and compliance with regulations.

The fuel consumption rate of the 60 Hz set is 0.55 gallons (2.1 liters) per hour, according to the provided manual excerpts. To determine how long a full tank will last, we need to divide the fuel tank capacity by the fuel consumption rate.

Fuel Tank Capacity: 5 gallons (18.9 liters)
Fuel Consumption Rate (60 Hz): 0.55 gallons (2.1 liters) per hour

Now, let's calculate the estimated duration:

5 gallons / 0.55 gallons per hour ≈ 9.09 hours

So, a full tank of fuel should last approximately 9.09 hours at the 60 Hz setting.

These switches are part of the Engine Starting System (Figure 1-3) and control the sequence of events that lead to engine starting.

1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

The manual you provided indicates a few potential issues that could be causing your engine to crank but not start in cold weather. Here are some steps you can take to troubleshoot and resolve the problem:

**1. Check the Master Switch:**

* **Page 69** mentions that if the **INTERRUPTER SWITCH** is closed, the engine will fail to crank. Make sure the master switch is in the "ON" position and fully engaged.

**2. Inspect for Starting Issues:**

* **Page 69** lists symptoms associated with starting problems, such as:
    * Engine stops when the master switch is released from the start position.
    * Engine stops suddenly.
    * Engine runs erratically or misfires.
    * Engine does not develop full power.
    * Engine knocks.
    * Excessive exhaust smoke (blue, white, black).

If your engine exhibits any of these symptoms, this could be indicative of a starting system issue. Check the battery, starter motor, wiring, and fuel system for potential problems.

**3. Check Engine Oil and Lubrication:**

* **Page 69** mentions low oil pressure as a potential issue. Check the engine oil level and ensure it's within the recommended range.

**4. Warm-Up Procedures:**

* Cold engines can be more difficult to start. Try the following warm-up procedures:
    * Let the engine idle for a few minutes after starting to allow the engine oil to circulate.
    * Use a block heater to warm the engine before attempting to start it.
    * If the problem persists, consider using a starting fluid or starting spray to help the engine ignite in cold temperatures.

**5. Professional Assistance:**

* If the engine still won't start after trying these steps, it's recommended to consult a qualified mechanic for a thorough inspection and diagnosis. They can identify any hidden issues and provide specific repairs or adjustments.


Remember to consult the complete manual for your specific engine model for detailed instructions and troubleshooting guidance.

To address the issue of your engine stopping immediately after you release the MASTER SWITCH from the START position, follow these steps:

1. **Check the Propeller Shaft and Propeller Shaft Bearing**: Ensure they are properly lubricated and free of damage.

2. **Check the Fuel Filter/Water Separator**: Inspect for dirt or debris. Refer to paragraph 3-3.6.2 for more information.

3. **Verify Proper Starting Procedure**: Make sure you are following the correct starting sequence as described in paragraphs 2-10.1 and 3-3. Hold the MASTER SWITCH in the START position until the engine reaches 25 psi (172 kPa).

4. **Check the Engine Starting System**: The engine starting system consists of several components, including the starter, 24-volt battery charging alternator, magnetic pickup, and related switches and relays. Ensure all these components are functioning correctly.

5. **Inspect for Interrupter Switch Issues**: If the interrupter switch is not functioning properly, the engine may not start as expected.

6. **Check for Exhaust System Issues**: Inspect the exhaust system for any signs of damage or malfunction, such as white or blue exhaust smoke, which could indicate a combustion issue.

7. **Examine the Lubricating System**: Low oil pressure can lead to engine failure. Check the oil pressure and ensure the lubricating system is functioning correctly.

8. **Notify Higher Maintenance Levels**: If the engine still fails to start after these checks, notify the next higher maintenance level.

If these steps do not resolve the issue, further investigation by a qualified technician may be necessary.

To address black exhaust smoke, follow these steps:

1. **Check for improper fuel type:** Black smoke often indicates insufficient combustion, which can be caused by using the wrong type of fuel. Refer to your vehicle's fuel specifications and ensure you're using the correct fuel type as listed in the owner's manual or vehicle documentation. 

2. **Inspect the fuel system:** If improper fuel type is ruled out, the issue could be related to the fuel system. Check for any leaks, blockages, or contamination in the fuel lines, filter, and injectors. Properly functioning fuel components are crucial for efficient combustion. 

3. **Examine the spark plugs:** Spark plugs play a vital role in igniting the air-fuel mixture. Inspect the spark plugs for wear, deposits, or damage. Faulty spark plugs can lead to incomplete combustion, resulting in black smoke. 

4. **Check the engine's performance:** Monitor the engine's performance, including fuel consumption, idle quality, and power output. If the engine is misfiring or not burning fuel efficiently, it may exhibit black smoke. 

5. **Consider additional factors:** 
   - **Engine temperature:** Engine overheating can affect combustion quality. Ensure the engine is operating at the correct temperature as specified in your vehicle's manual. 
   - **Air intake system:** Inspect the air filter and intake system for any blockages or damage. Proper air supply is essential for complete combustion. 
   - **Exhaust system:** While not mentioned in the excerpt, ensure the exhaust system is not clogged or malfunctioning, as it can impact combustion and smoke production. 

6. **Seek professional assistance:** If the issue persists, or if you're unsure about any component, it's recommended to consult a qualified mechanic. They can diagnose the problem accurately and provide appropriate solutions.

If you are experiencing no voltage at the convenience receptacle, follow these steps:

1. **Check the Generator Set:**
   - Start the generator set if it is not operating. Refer to Paragraph 2-10 for instructions.

2. **Ensure Load Management:**
   - Ensure the load does not exceed the maximum rating of 10 Amps. Decrease the load if necessary.

3. **Reset the Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GFCI):**
   - Open the control panel and inspect the circuit breaker on the side of the GFCI device. If it is tripped, reset it.
   - Check the fuse on the black wire of the GFCI for generator sets with contract number DAAK01-88-D-D080.

4. **Verify Reset Button:**
   - Check the reset button for a red band. If the red band is visible, push the reset button. If the GFCI cannot be reset, consult a higher maintenance level.

These steps should help identify and resolve the issue with the voltage at the convenience receptacle.

Weight Control 
Weight is a major factor in airplane construction and 
operation, and it demands respect from all pilots and 
particular diligence by all maintenance personnel. Excessive 
weight reduces the efficiencyof an aircraft and the available 
safety margin if an emergency condition should arise.
When an aircraft is designed, it is made as light as the 
required structural strength allows, and the wings or rotors are 
designed to support the maximum allowable weight. When 
the weight of an aircraft is increased, the wings or rotors must 
produce additional lift and the structure must support not 
only the additional static loads, but also the dynamic loads 
imposed by flight maneuvers. For example, the wings of a 
3,000-pound airplane must support 3,000 pounds in level 
flight, but when the airplane is turned smoothly and sharply 
using a bank angle of 60°, the dynamic load requires the 
wings to support twice this or 6,000 pounds.
Severe uncoordinated maneuvers or flight into turbulence 
can impose dynamic loads on the structure great enough 
to cause failure. In accordance with Title 14 of the Code

The Center of Gravity (CG) on a swept-wing airplane moves in the following way as fuel is used from the outboard tanks:

As fuel is used from the outboard tanks, the CG shifts forward. Conversely, as fuel is used from the inboard tanks, the CG shifts aft.

This fuel imbalance is a critical aspect of swept-wing airplane operation, as it directly affects the aircraft's longitudinal balance. Proper fuel management and scheduling are essential to ensure the CG remains within safe limits throughout the flight.

Weight Control for Aircraft Other Than 
Fixed and Rotor-wing
Some light aircraft utilize different methods of determining 
weight and balance from the traditional fixedand rotor-wing 
aircraft. These aircraft achieve flight control by methods 
different from the fixed-wing airplane or helicopter. Most 
notable of these are weight-shift control (WSC) aircraft (also 
known as trikes), powered parachutes, and balloons. These 
aircraft typically do not specify either an EWCG or a CG 
range. They require only a certified or approved maximum 
weight. To understand why this is so, a look at how flight
control is achieved is helpful.
Airplanes and WSC aircraft control flightunder the influenc  
of the same four forces (lift, gravity, thrust, and drag), and 
around the same three axes (pitch, yaw, and roll). However, 
each aircraft accomplishes this control in a very different 
manner. This difference helps explain why the fixed-wing
airplane requires an established weight and a known CG, 
whereas the WSC aircraft only requires the known weight.
The fixed-wing airplane has movable controls that alter lift 
on various airfoil surfaces to vary pitch, roll, and yaw. In 
turn, these changes in lift affect the characteristics of the 
flight parameters. Weight normally decreases in flight due 
to fuel consumption, and the airplane CG changes with this 
weight reduction. An airplane utilizes

the maximum allowable baggage.
Under these loading conditions, the CG is located at +45.8, 
which is ahead of the aft limit of +46.0. [Figure 7-10] With 
only the pilot in front of the aft CG limit and maximum of all 
items behind the aft limit, the CG is at +45.8 inches, which 
is ahead of the aft limit of +46.0 inches.
Ballast
It is possible to load most modern airplanes so the CG 
shifts outside of the allowable limit. Placards and loading 
instructions in the weight and balance data inform the pilot 
of the restrictions that prevent such a shift from occurring. 
A typical placard in the baggage compartment of an airplane 
is shown in Figure 7-11. When the CG of an aircraft falls 
outside of the limits, it can usually be brought back in by 
using ballast.

Weight and Balance
Aircraft such as balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC do 
not require weight and balance computations because the load 
is suspended below the lifting mechanism. The CG range in 
these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG 
limits. For example, the rear seat position and fuel of a WSC 
aircraft are as close as possible to the hang point with the 
aircraft in a suspended attitude. Thus, load variations have 
little effect on the CG. This also holds true for lighter-than-
air aircraft, such as a balloon basket or gondola. While it is 
difficult to exceed CG limits in these aircraft, pilots should 
never overload an aircraft, as doing so may cause structural 
damage and/or failures. 
Weight affects performance; therefore, pilots should calculate 
weight and remain within the manufacturer’s established 
limits at all times.
WSC Aircraft
WSC aircraft are one- and two-place aircraft that exceed the 
criteria of an ultra-light vehicle but do meet the criteria of an 
LSA. The definitionfor WSC can be found in 14 CFR part 1.

Airplanes with tandem seating normally have a limitation

As an aircraft ages, its weight usually increases due to debris 
and dirt collecting in hard-to-reach locations and moisture 
absorbed in the cabin insulation. This increase in weight is 
normally small, but it can be determined only by accurately 
weighing the aircraft.
Changes of fixed equipment may have a major effect upon 
the weight of the aircraft. Many aircraft are overloaded by 
the installation of extra radios or instruments. Fortunately, 
the replacement of older, heavy electronic equipment with 
newer, lighter types results in a weight reduction. This 
weight change, however helpful, can cause the CG to shift,

balance record.

All scales for aviation use, manual or electronic, must be

between calibration checks is 12 months; however, this period 
may be reduced by an airworthiness authority dependent on 
the conditions of use. Scales in daily use may require a shorter

proper calibration and testing. 
Preparation for Weighing
In general, weight procedures may vary with the aircraft 
and types of weight equipment employed. The weighing 
procedure contained in the manufacturer’s maintenance 
manual should be followed for each particular aircraft. The 
major considerations in preparing an aircraft for weighing 
are described in the following paragraphs.
Scale Preparation
Mechanical and electronic scales shall be inspected prior to 
use and set to zero. This is done by adding and removing 
a weight, then rechecking for zero. This process should be 
repeated until a steady zero setting is obtained. The scales 
should be located in the same environment in which they

maintained by the operator. It is potentially unsafe to fail to 
reweigh an aircraft after it has been modified
When weighing large aircraft, compliance with the relevant 
manuals, operations specifications, or management 
specification is required to ensure that weight and balance 
requirements specified in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) 
are met in accordance with approved limits. This provides 
information to the flight crew that allows the maximum 
payload to be carried safely. 
The aircraft should be weighed in still air or an enclosed 
building after the aircraft has been cleaned. Ensure that the 
aircraft is in a configuration for weighing with regard to 
flightcontrols, unusable fuel, ballast, oil and other operating 
fluids, and equipment as required by the controlling weight 
and balance procedure.
Large aircraft are not usually raised off the floor on jacks 
for weighing; they are weighed on ramp-type scales. The 
scales must be properly calibrated, zeroed, and used in 
accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Each scale 
should be periodically checked for accuracy as recommended 
in the manufacturer’s calibration schedule, either by the 
manufacturer or by a recognized facility, such as a civil 
department of weights and measures. If no manufacturer’s 
schedule is available, the period between calibrations should 
not exceed 12 months.

Empty Weight CG (EWCG)

Weighing aircraft with accurately calibrated scales is the only

are platform and load cell.
Platform scales [Figure 3-1] or ramp wheel scales

pounds since the weight on each wheel rarely exceeds this 
figure
Load cell scales [Figure 3-3] are also a reliable means to 
weigh aircraft and are typically cheaper than the platform 
type.Using load cell scales allows for the aircraft to be set 
up and weighed in its level flight attitude. With this method, 
the aircraft is placed on jacks with electronic load cells 
placed between the jack and the jack pad on the aircraft. 
The aircraft is raised on the jacks until the wheels or skids 
are off the floor and the aircraft is in a level flight attitude. 
The weight measured by each load cell is indicated on the 
control panel. Jacking an aircraft off the ground from all

When the aircraft is properly prepared for weighing, roll it

Determine the moment index of each of the main-

weighing point by multiplying its net weight, in 
pounds, by its distance from the datum, in inches.

3.

the three weighing points and the total moment index 
by adding the moment indexes of each point.
4.	
Divide the total moment index by the total weight and 
multiply the result by the reduction factor. This gives 
the CG in inches from the datum.

edge of the mean aerodynamic chord (LEMAC) 
by subtracting the distance between the datum and 
LEMAC from the distance between the

To determine the minimum fuel for a forward adverse-load CG check, the following steps are outlined:

1. **Determine the minimum fuel quantity:** The minimum fuel quantity is calculated as the quantity needed for one-half hour of operation at rated maximum continuous power. For aviation gasoline, this is 1/12 gallon per METO horsepower.

2. **Convert the fuel quantity to pounds:** Since aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon, the minimum fuel quantity in pounds is calculated by multiplying the fuel quantity in gallons by the weight per gallon (1/12 gallon * METO horsepower * 6 pounds/gallon).

3. **Example calculation:** The manual provides an example where the METO horsepower is 230. The minimum fuel quantity is then calculated as (1/12 * 230) * 6 = 115 pounds.

4. **Use the minimum fuel in the CG calculation:** The minimum fuel is included in the weight and balance calculation for the forward adverse-load CG check.

5. **Consider the loading conditions:** The manual emphasizes that the loading conditions, including the pilot's weight and the minimum fuel, must be considered when calculating the CG.

By following these steps, the minimum fuel required for a forward adverse-load CG check can be determined and included in the weight and balance calculations.

To make and mark permanent ballast, follow these steps:

1. **Determine the required ballast weight:** Calculate the weight of the permanent ballast using the formula provided in Figure 7-13. The formula is based on the aircraft's empty weight and the distance the center of gravity (CG) needs to be adjusted.

   * **Formula:** Ballast needed = (Aircraft empty weight) × (1 - (Distance between ballast and the affected limit / CG range for the loaded weight))

   * **Example:** For an aircraft with an empty weight of 1,876 pounds and an EWCG (+32.2) that needs to be adjusted to +33.0 within a CG range of +33.0 to +46.0, the calculation would be:

     Ballast needed = 1,876 × (1 - (228 - 33) / (2250 - 1876)) ≈ 7.7 pounds

2. **Construct the ballast:** Create a block of lead with the calculated weight. Ensure it is painted red as per the manual's instructions.

3. **Mark the ballast:** Clearly mark the lead block with the following:
   * "Permanent Ballast—Do Not Remove"
   * This warning is crucial to ensure the ballast is not accidentally removed.

4. **Secure the ballast:** Attach the lead block to the aircraft structure, specifically to a robust component like a bulkhead (as mentioned in the example, at fuselage station 228), ensuring it is rigidly fixed and won't be dislodged during flight maneuvers or rough landings.

5. **Documentation:** Record the weight, location, and purpose of the installed permanent ballast for future reference and maintenance.

Between reweighings, an aircraft's Operational Empty Weight (OEW) must be reestablished by calculation under certain conditions as outlined in the manual. The OEW and CG position of each aircraft should be reestablished at the reweighing, and whenever the cumulative change to the weight and balance log is more than plus or minus one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the maximum landing weight, or whenever the cumulative change in the CG position exceeds one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the MAC. This applies to all aircraft, including rotorcraft and those that do not have a MAC-based CG envelope. 

In addition, whenever an aircraft has undergone extensive repair or major alteration, it should be reweighed and a new weight and balance record started. This is to ensure that the aircraft's weight and CG location are accurately reflected in the current approved aircraft flight manual or issued operating limitations.

To determine if the air cleaner element needs servicing, the operator should inspect the following:

- **Look for **restriction indicator for clogged air cleaner element**:** According to the manual, the restriction indicator is a crucial visual clue. If the indicator shows signs of clogging, it's a clear indication that the air cleaner element needs attention.
- **Inspect for **leaks, corrosion, and missing parts**:** The manual emphasizes inspecting for leaks, corrosion, and any missing parts in the air cleaner assembly. These issues can lead to reduced performance and potential damage to the system.
- **Check for **loose, damaged, or missing parts**:** Inspecting the air cleaner assembly for loose, damaged, or missing parts is essential. This includes checking the grounding rod assembly and the connections to ensure they are secure and intact.
- **Examine **the exhaust/intake system**:** While not explicitly mentioned for the air cleaner element, inspecting the exhaust and intake systems as a whole is important. Look for any signs of damage, corrosion, or excessive wear that could be affecting the air cleaner's performance.

If any of these inspections reveal issues, the operator should take appropriate action and service the air cleaner element accordingly.

The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the

The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here are the steps to check when the engine starts but stops as soon as the MASTER SWITCH is released from the START position:

**Step 1: Check the Engine Starting Process**

* Ensure the DEAD CRANK switch is in the NORMAL position.
* Push in the DC Control power circuit breaker.
* Ensure the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH is in the OUT position.
* Move the MASTER SWITCH to the START position.

**Step 2: Hold the MASTER SWITCH in the START Position**

* Hold the MASTER SWITCH in the START position until the engine reaches 25 psi (172 kPa) of pressure. Refer to Paragraph 2-10.1.3.3 for more information.

**Step 3: Check for the Following Issues**

* **Fuel System:** Check the fuel filter and water separator for dirt. Refer to Paragraph 3-3.6.2 for more information.
* **Engine Control:** If the engine still fails to start after completing these steps, notify the next higher maintenance level.
* **Other Potential Issues:** If you suspect other issues, consult the appropriate sections of the manual, such as those related to the exhaust system, lubricating system, or other engine components.

**Troubleshooting Additional Issues**

* **Interrupter Switch:** Ensure the interrupter switch is closed. (Refer to Page 69)
* **Cranking Relay:** Check the cranking relay and its connections.
* **Battery Power:** Verify the batteries are functioning properly and have sufficient charge.

repeats.answer:
To troubleshoot the issue of no voltage at the convenience receptacle, follow these steps:

1. **Start the Generator Set (if not operating)**: Ensure the generator set is operational by following the instructions in paragraph 2-10 of the manual.

2. **Ensure Load Does Not Exceed Maximum Rating**: Verify that the load on the convenience receptacle does not exceed the maximum 10 Amp rating. Decrease the load if necessary.

3. **Reset the Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GCI)**:
   - Open the control panel and inspect the circuit breaker on the side of the GCI device.
   - If the circuit breaker is tripped, reset it.
   - Check the fuse on the black wire of the GCI for the specific generator sets (contract number DAAK01-88-D-D080). If the fuse is blown, replace it.

4. **Check Reset Button for Red Band**:
   - If the GCI cannot be reset, inspect the reset button for a visible red band.
   - If the red band is visible, push the reset button.

The load factor for the structure of a normal category airplane is 3.8 times its weight. This means that for every pound of weight added to the airplane, the structure must be able to support 3.8 pounds.

Comparatively, the utility category requires a load factor of 4.4 times its weight, while the acrobatic category requires a load factor of 6.0 times its weight. Therefore, the normal category airplane has a lower load factor compared to the utility and acrobatic categories.

Weight Control for Aircraft Other Than 
Fixed and Rotor-wing
Some light aircraft utilize different methods of determining 
weight and balance from the traditional fixedand rotor-wing 
aircraft. These aircraft achieve flight control by methods 
different from the fixed-wing airplane or helicopter. Most 
notable of these are weight-shift control (WSC) aircraft (also 
known as trikes), powered parachutes, and balloons. These 
aircraft typically do not specify either an EWCG or a CG 
range. They require only a certified or approved maximum 
weight. To understand why this is so, a look at how flight
control is achieved is helpful.
Airplanes and WSC aircraft control flightunder the influenc  
of the same four forces (lift, gravity, thrust, and drag), and 
around the same three axes (pitch, yaw, and roll). However, 
each aircraft accomplishes this control in a very different 
manner. This difference helps explain why the fixed-wing
airplane requires an established weight and a known CG, 
whereas the WSC aircraft only requires the known weight.
The fixed-wing airplane has movable controls that alter lift 
on various airfoil surfaces to vary pitch, roll, and yaw. In 
turn, these changes in lift affect the characteristics of the 
flight parameters. Weight normally decreases in flight due 
to fuel consumption, and the airplane CG changes with this

All scales for aviation use, manual or electronic, must be

between calibration checks is 12 months; however, this period 
may be reduced by an airworthiness authority dependent on 
the conditions of use. Scales in daily use may require a shorter

Preparation for Weighing
In general, weight procedures may vary with the aircraft 
and types of weight equipment employed. The weighing 
procedure contained in the manufacturer’s maintenance 
manual should be followed for each particular aircraft. The 
major considerations in preparing an aircraft for weighing 
are described in the following paragraphs.
Scale Preparation
Mechanical and electronic scales shall be inspected prior to 
use and set to zero. This is done by adding and removing 
a weight, then rechecking for zero. This process should be 
repeated until a steady zero setting is obtained. The scales 
should be located in the same environment in which they

When weighing large aircraft, compliance with the relevant 
manuals, operations specifications, or management 
specification is required to ensure that weight and balance 
requirements specified in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) 
are met in accordance with approved limits. This provides 
information to the flight crew that allows the maximum 
payload to be carried safely. 
The aircraft should be weighed in still air or an enclosed 
building after the aircraft has been cleaned. Ensure that the 
aircraft is in a configuration for weighing with regard to 
flightcontrols, unusable fuel, ballast, oil and other operating 
fluids, and equipment as required by the controlling weight 
and balance procedure.
Large aircraft are not usually raised off the floor on jacks 
for weighing; they are weighed on ramp-type scales. The 
scales must be properly calibrated, zeroed, and used in 
accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Each scale 
should be periodically checked for accuracy as recommended 
in the manufacturer’s calibration schedule, either by the 
manufacturer or by a recognized facility, such as a civil 
department of weights and measures. If no manufacturer’s 
schedule is available, the period between calibrations should 
not exceed 12 months.

Equipment for Weighing
Weighing aircraft with accurately calibrated scales is the only 
sure method of obtaining an accurate empty weight and CG 
location. The two basic types of scales used to weigh aircraft 
are platform and load cell.
Platform scales [Figure 3-1] or ramp wheel scales 
[Figure 3-2] (usually a form or modified version of the 
platform scale) are low profi e, easy to handle, safe, and 
reliable. Tow or push the aircraft wheels or skids onto the 
scale pad at ground level. With one scale per wheel, each 
device should be capable of measuring up to at least 60,000 
pounds since the weight on each wheel rarely exceeds this 
figure
Load cell scales [Figure 3-3] are also a reliable means to 
weigh aircraft and are typically cheaper than the platform 
type.Using load cell scales allows for the aircraft to be set 
up and weighed in its level flight attitude. With this method, 
the aircraft is placed on jacks with electronic load cells 
placed between the jack and the jack pad on the aircraft. 
The aircraft is raised on the jacks until the wheels or skids 
are off the floor and the aircraft is in a level flight attitude. 
The weight measured by each load cell is indicated on the 
control panel. Jacking an aircraft off the ground from all 
load points can be an inconvenience, as well as a safety 
risk, which some operators would rather avoid by opting for

Empty Weight CG (EWCG)
When the aircraft is properly prepared for weighing, roll it 
onto the scales, and level it. The weights are measured at 
three weighing points: the two main wheel points and the 
nosewheel point. The empty weight and empty weight CG 
(EWCG) are determined by using the following steps with 
the results recorded in the weight and balance record for use

Determine the moment index of each of the main-

weighing point by multiplying its net weight, in 
pounds, by its distance from the datum, in inches.

3.	
Determine the total weight by adding the net weight of 
the three weighing points and the total moment index 
by adding the moment indexes of each point.
4.	
Divide the total moment index by the total weight and 
multiply the result by the reduction factor. This gives 
the CG in inches from the datum.
5.	
Determine the distance of the CG behind the leading 
edge of the mean aerodynamic chord (LEMAC) 
by subtracting the distance between the datum and 
LEMAC from the distance between the

To determine the minimum fuel required for a forward adverse-load CG check, you can follow these steps based on the provided manual excerpts:

1. Determine the METO (Maximum Takeoff) horsepower of the aircraft. You can find this information in the manual or by consulting other sources.

2. Calculate the minimum fuel needed for one-half hour of operation at rated maximum continuous power. This is given as 1/12 gallon for each METO horsepower.

3. Convert the fuel volume to weight. Aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon. Multiply the fuel volume (in gallons) by 6 to get the weight in pounds.

4. In the provided example, the METO horsepower is 230. Using the formula from step 2: 1/12 gallon per METO horsepower, you calculate the minimum fuel volume as: (1/12) * 230 = 19.17 gallons.

5. Convert the minimum fuel volume to weight using the specific gravity of aviation gasoline (6 pounds per gallon). The minimum fuel weight is: 19.17 gallons * 6 pounds/gallon = **115 pounds**.

6. In the context of the forward adverse-load CG check, this minimum fuel quantity is used.

So, for a forward adverse-load CG check, the minimum fuel is **115 pounds** of aviation gasoline.

To make and mark permanent ballast, you should follow these steps:

1. **Determine the required ballast weight:**
   - Calculate the amount of ballast needed using the formula:
     Ballast needed = (Empty weight of the aircraft) × (Distance out of limits) / (Distance between the ballast location and the affected CG limit)

2. **Construct the ballast:**
   - Use blocks of lead, as they are commonly used for permanent ballast.
   - Ensure the lead blocks are painted red, as mentioned in the manual.

3. **Mark the ballast:**
   - Clearly mark the lead blocks with the following: "Permanent Ballast—Do Not Remove."

4. **Attach the ballast securely:**
   - Attach the lead blocks to the aircraft structure, specifically to the bulkhead at the specified fuselage station, ensuring they are rigidly fixed and won't be dislodged during flight maneuvers or rough landings.

5. **Ensure structural integrity:**
   - Verify that the attachment points are strong enough to support the weight of the ballast without compromising the aircraft's structural integrity.

6. **Location:**
   - Place the ballast at the location that will bring the CG within the allowable range. In the example provided, the ballast is installed at fuselage station 228 to move the EWCG from +32.2 to +33.0.

Between reweighings, a large aircraft's Operational Empty Weight (OEW) must be reestablished by calculation when the cumulative change in the weight and balance log exceeds the specified limits, or when the cumulative change in the Center of Gravity (CG) position exceeds the specified limits. The limits are as follows:

- **Weight and Balance Log Limits:** More than plus or minus one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the maximum landing weight.
- **CG Position Limits:** One-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the MAC (Maximum Allowable Cabin) for aircraft with a MAC-based CG envelope, or one-half of 1 percent (0.5 percent) of the total CG range for rotorcraft and aircraft without a MAC-based CG envelope.

It's important to note that these calculations should be based on the known weight and CG location of the modifications, according to the manual excerpts provided. If the weight and CG location of the modifications are unknown, the aircraft must be reweighed.

Additionally, the OEW and CG position should also be reestablished at the reweighing, ensuring compliance with the specified limits and providing accurate information for flight crew operations.

To determine if the airplane is properly loaded for landing in the given single-engine sample loading problem with a total weight of 3,027 lb, follow these steps:

1. **Determine the Loaded Weight and CG:**
   - According to the manual, the total weight of the loaded aircraft is 3,027 pounds.
   - The Center of Gravity (CG) for the loaded aircraft should be within the allowable limits.

2. **Use the CG Limits Chart:**
   - The CG limits chart, as mentioned on page 50, helps determine if the airplane is properly loaded.
   - Draw a vertical line upward from the CG of 43.54 inches (a positive result indicates a CG aft of the datum).
   - Draw a horizontal line to the right from the loaded weight of 3,027 pounds.
   - These lines should intersect within the envelope defined by the solid black line indicating CG limits at or below the maximum weight for landing (2,950 lb).

3. **Analysis:**
   - The manual states, "These lines cross inside the envelope, which shows the airplane is properly loaded for takeoff, but 77 pounds over the maximum weight for landing."

4. **Consider the Adverse-Load CG Check:**
   - If the aircraft is overloaded for landing, an adverse-load CG check must be performed.
   - This involves using the weights and moments of the load, occupants, and essential items to ensure the CG is within the allowable limits.

5. **Conclusion:**
   - Since the airplane is 77 pounds over the maximum weight for landing, it is not properly loaded for landing. The pilot would need to take corrective action to reduce the weight before landing. This could include removing excess baggage or fuel.

It seems like you've provided a lot of information about aircraft weight and balance calculations, and then you've asked to compute the weight and balance using the loading graph in Figure 5-6. However, the actual computation for the specific case of 390 gallons of Jet A fuel by interpolating between 6.7 lb/gal and 6.8 lb/gal was already provided in your initial list of weights and moment/100.

To follow your instructions, I will use the provided information to compute the weight and balance.

1. **Determine the weights and moment/100 for 390 gallons of Jet A fuel by interpolating between those for 6.7 lb/gal and 6.8 lb/gal.**

   - Weight: 390 gallons * 6.75 lb/gal = 2625 pounds (Interpolated between 6.7 lb/gal and 6.8 lb/gal)

According to the manual, here are the indicators that the air cleaner element may need servicing:

* **Restriction indicator for clogged air cleaner element**: The manual explicitly mentions that you should inspect the restriction indicator for clogged air cleaner element. This would be a visual indication that the air cleaner element is not functioning properly and needs attention.

* **Leaks, damaged, or missing parts**: While not directly mentioning the air cleaner element, the manual notes that leaks, damaged, or missing parts in the exhaust/intake system generally indicate that the system may need maintenance, which could include the air cleaner element.

* **Clogged air cleaner element**: The "Not Fully Mission Capable" section explicitly states that clogged air cleaner element is a reason for the generator set not being fully mission capable. This is a clear indicator that the air cleaner element needs servicing.

Therefore, the operator should pay close attention to the restriction indicator, inspect for any visible damage or clogging, and be aware that a clogged air cleaner element can render the generator set not fully mission capable.

It seems like the manual excerpt you provided doesn't explicitly mention a specific solution for when the engine cranks but won't start in cold weather. However, based on the context of the excerpt, here are a few potential issues and solutions that might be relevant:

1. **Interrupter Switch**: The excerpt mentions that if the interrupter switch is closed, the engine might not start. Make sure the interrupter switch is open.

2. **Cold Weather**: Cold weather can affect the engine's ability to start. Ensure that the fuel system is not clogged or frozen, and that the fuel filter is clean and functioning properly.

3. **Battery**: Cold temperatures can also affect the battery's performance. Check the battery voltage and ensure it is within the recommended range.

4. **Engine Oil**: Cold temperatures can make it harder for the engine to start. Ensure that the engine oil is at the correct viscosity for cold temperatures.

5. **Spark Plugs**: Cold temperatures can affect the spark plugs' ability to create a spark. Check the spark plugs for wear and tear, and replace them if necessary.

6. **Fuel System**: Cold temperatures can cause fuel to gel or freeze. Ensure that the fuel system is not clogged or frozen, and that the fuel filter is clean and functioning properly.

7. **Ignition System**: Check the ignition system for any issues, such as faulty spark plugs, ignition coils, or distributor caps.

8. **Engine Sensors**: Ensure that all engine sensors, such as the temperature sensor and mass airflow sensor, are functioning properly.

If none of these solutions work, it might be best to consult a professional mechanic for further diagnosis and repair.

SECTION Ill . TECHNICAL PRINCIPLES OF OPERATION
1-10 
This section contains functional descriptions of the
generator set and explains how the controls and indicators
1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

If there is no voltage at the convenience receptacle, you should follow these steps according to the provided manual excerpts:

1. **Open the control panel and inspect the circuit breaker on the side of the Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter (GCI) device.**
2. If the circuit breaker is tripped, **reset it**.
3. **Check the fuse on the black wire of the GCI** for the specific generator sets, which have a contract number of DAAK01-88-D-D080.
4. **Check the reset button for a red band.** If the red band is visible, **push the reset button**.
5. If the GCI cannot be reset, **refer the issue to the next higher maintenance level**.

Remember, the manual explicitly warns about the dangers of working with power and emphasizes the importance of following these steps to avoid electrical hazards.
